headline: Maine’s in-person absentee voting window opens for Nov. 3 election
dek: Mainers can now vote at their municipal clerk’s office without an excuse, with registration and ballot-return deadlines approaching later this month.
body: Maine’s in-person absentee voting window is now open for the Nov. 3 general election, giving voters a way to cast a ballot at their town office or city hall before Election Day. The 30-day period began Oct. 4 under the state’s election calendar and runs through close of business Thursday, Oct. 29, according to the [Maine Secretary of State’s election update](https://www3.maine.gov/sos/news/general-election-two-months-away-secretary-states-office-provides-update-maine-election-1).

The opening is a statewide administrative milestone, not a separate election. Maine uses no-excuse absentee voting, so a registered voter does not need to explain why they cannot vote at the polls. The [Secretary of State’s voter guide](https://www.maine.gov/sos/elections-voting/state-of-maine-voter-guide) says ballots are available at municipal clerk offices and that voters who cast an absentee ballot in person do not need to complete an application first. Local clerks control the exact hours and locations, so voters should check the [state’s municipal office-hours and drop-box list](https://www.maine.gov/sos/elections-voting/upcoming-elections) and confirm details with their town or city before going.

The first-day demand comes as the state’s absentee system is already active. As of Friday, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said Maine had received just over 70,000 absentee-ballot requests, according to [Spectrum News Maine’s Monday report](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/me/maine/news/2026/10/05/voting-early). The report said a little more than 45,000 ballots had been issued and 793 had been returned and accepted at that point. Those are processing figures, not turnout projections: a request is not a cast ballot, and the numbers can change as municipal clerks enter new information.

Voters who prefer to receive a ballot at home can request one online, through their town office or city hall, or with a paper application. The request generally must reach the municipal clerk by close of business Thursday, Oct. 29, three business days before the election, unless a special circumstance applies. The state warns that only ballots received by 8 p.m. on Election Day are counted, regardless of the postmark. Many communities also provide secured drop boxes, and Maine’s election materials include a ballot-status lookup tool.

The other important date for people who are not yet registered is Tuesday, Oct. 13. The state says online registrations and registrations submitted by mail or a third person must reach the voter’s town or city by the close of business that day, 21 days before the election. Registration through a Bureau of Motor Vehicles office remains available through Tuesday, Oct. 27. Maine also allows in-person registration through the close of the polls on Election Day, although voters should allow time for the clerk or polling place to verify their information.

Maine’s statewide election page lists the Nov. 3 contest, municipal voting-place information and the current absentee-ballot request form. The Secretary of State’s voter guide says residents must be U.S. citizens with an established home in Maine to register, and must be at least 18 to vote in the general election. It directs voters to their town office or city hall for local polling-place details; all voting places close at 8 p.m. on Election Day, while opening times vary by community.

Absentee ballots may be processed before Election Day in municipalities that follow the state’s early-processing rules, but the Secretary of State says they cannot be counted until after 8 p.m. on Nov. 3. That distinction matters as more voters use the early option: clerks can prepare ballots and secure them, while the public result still waits for the legal counting period. The state says early processing may begin up to seven days before the election and can be observed under published procedures.

Bellows told Spectrum News that Maine ranked first nationally in voter participation in the 2022 midterm election and third in 2024, while the state’s June primary produced record turnout. Those comparisons describe Maine’s recent participation, not a forecast for November. For voters, the immediate task is more practical: confirm registration, check the municipal clerk’s hours, request or cast an absentee ballot before the applicable deadline, and leave enough time for a ballot to reach officials by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
